facts.fact_text: The picket took place as planned between 11 a.m. and 1 p.m. on 19 March 2009.
According to the applicant, the picket on 19 March 2009 was peaceful.
The police report of 19 March 2009 noted that there had been no violation of public order during the picket.
On 4 April 2009 a police officer of the Prymorsky District Police Department of Odessa drew up an administrative offence report in the applicant's presence.
The administrative offence report of 4 April 2009 indicated that on 19 March 2009 the applicant had organised and held a picket in violation of Article 185-1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The administrative offence report of 4 April 2009 was referred to a court.
On 15 May 2009 the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa examined the applicant's case.

The Prymorsky District Court of Odessa held that the applicant was in breach of Article 185-1 of the Code of Administrative Offences because he had not complied with the ten-day notification requirement.
In its judgment of 15 May 2009, the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa fined the applicant 170 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH) (approximately 17 euros (EUR)).

The Odessa City Council's letter of 17 March 2009 mentioned that the 1988 Decree (Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 on the procedure for organisation and holding of meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the USSR) was still in force.

The Odessa City Council's letter of 17 March 2009 informed the applicant that untimely notification about the picket could be considered a violation of the procedure for holding meetings under paragraph 2 of the 1988 Decree (Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988).

The Odessa City Council's letter of 17 March 2009 informed the applicant that the person responsible for untimely notification could be held administratively liable under Article 185-1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Prymorsky District Court of Odessa based its findings on the 1988 Decree (Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988), which provided that an application to hold an assembly had to be lodged with the relevant authority at least ten days in advance.

In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine held that the provisions of Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine on timely notification to executive authorities or bodies of local self-government about planned meetings, rallies, marches or demonstrations shall be understood to mean that organisers must inform the above-mentioned authorities in advance, that is, within a reasonable time prior to the date of the planned event.

The Constitutional Court of Ukraine's decision of 19 April 2001 held that the notification time-limits should not restrict the right of citizens under Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine, but should serve as a guarantee of this right and at the same time provide the relevant executive authorities or bodies of local self-government with an opportunity to take measures to ensure that citizens may freely hold meetings, rallies, marches and demonstrations and to protect public order and the rights and freedoms of others.

The Constitutional Court of Ukraine's decision of 19 April 2001 held that specifying the exact deadlines for timely notification with regard to the particularities of different forms of peaceful assembly, the number of participants, the venue, and the time of the event is a matter for legislative regulation.

In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine considered an application by the Ministry of the Interior of Ukraine for an official interpretation of the provisions of Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine regarding timely notification to executive authorities or bodies of local self-government of planned meetings, rallies, marches or demonstrations.

The Constitutional Court of Ukraine's decision of 19 April 2001 noted that the current legislation of Ukraine does not provide for a specific time-limit within which the executive authorities or bodies of local self-government are to be notified about planned meetings, rallies, marches or demonstrations.

In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine held that the provisions of Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine on timely notification to executive authorities or bodies of local self-government about planned meetings, rallies, marches or demonstrations shall be understood to mean that organisers must inform the above-mentioned authorities in advance, that is, within a reasonable time prior to the date of the planned event.

The Information Note of April 2012 of the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine stated that judicial practice contained instances of cases restricting the right to peaceful assembly being decided on the basis of the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations laid down by the Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 No. 9306-XI, and that this approach is incorrect.

The Information Note of April 2012 of the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine stated that the norms of the 1988 Decree establish the procedure for authorising (registering) peaceful assembly and empower the authorities and bodies of local self-government to ban such events, whereas the norms of the Constitution of Ukraine provide for a procedure whereby the authorities are notified that a gathering is to be held and provide that only the courts have power to ban a peaceful gathering.

The Information Note of April 2012 of the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine stated that the 1988 Decree (Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988) should not be applied by courts when deciding cases concerning the right to peaceful assembly.

In its decision of 16 May 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that the 1988 Decree conflicted with the Constitution of Ukraine as it required the organisers to seek permission to hold a demonstration and authorised the executive authorities to ban such an event, whereas Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provided that the authorities should be notified that a demonstration was being planned and empowered only the judicial authorities to place restrictions on the organisation thereof.

In its decision of 16 May 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that in its decision of 19 April 2001 the Constitutional Court of Ukraine had not referred to the 1988 Decree as a normative act which should apply in Ukraine to the legal relations under consideration.

In its decision of 16 May 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that the file contained no documents proving that notification about the demonstration less than 10 days in advance had not allowed the police to ensure public order during the demonstration and that the holding of such an event could create a real risk of riots or crimes or endanger the health of the population and imperil the rights and freedoms of others.

In its decision of 16 May 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal concluded that the judgment of the Kyiv Administrative Court of 29 November 2011 was incompatible with Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine and Article 11 of the Convention.

In a decision of 11 October 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal quashed a judgment of the Kyiv Administrative Court which had restricted the freedom of peaceful assembly in respect of a number of political and non-governmental organisations upon an application by the Kyiv City State Administration.

In its decision of 11 October 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that in deciding the case the first-instance court (Kyiv Administrative Court) had had regard to the provisions of the 1988 Decree (Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988), whereas since 1996 the question of holding peaceful gatherings had been regulated by the Constitution of Ukraine.

In its decision of 11 October 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal stated that the 1988 Decree conflicted with the Constitution of Ukraine as it provided for a procedure for seeking permission to hold a demonstration.

In its decision of 11 October 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal stated that the 1988 Decree concerned the holding of demonstrations in a non-existent country (the USSR), regulated relations between the citizens of the USSR and the executive committees of the Soviets of People's Deputies, and considered demonstrations on the basis of their compatibility with the Constitution of the USSR and the constitutions of the union and autonomous republics, that is, non-existent constitutions of non-existent subjects.

In its decision of 11 October 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that under the Constitution of Ukraine human rights and freedoms, and the relevant safeguards, could be defined only by the laws of Ukraine.
